title: etc-fp-bitexact, explained
h1: Will two vendors' floating-point handoffs agree, bit for bit?
lead: A small, Mathlib-free Lean library that turns two invented interface specs into one yes-or-no question about 16-bit floating-point bit patterns, and then settles it. When the answer is no, the proof names a concrete input that breaks it. In this demo the culprit is the tiniest subnormal number, 0x0001, which a spec that says nothing about subnormal handling allows to be flushed to zero. Every “yes” is re-checked from a stored SAT certificate, so nobody needs to re-run the solver.
desc: A plain-English tour of etc-fp-bitexact by Evolving Technologies Corporation: a Lean 4 demo that checks bit-exact compatibility of invented binary16 interface specs with bv_decide and replays stored LRAT certificates without a SAT solver.
startNote: Start with the compatibility statement, the one question every Configuration-1 verdict asks. Then read the four verdicts in order: compatible, divergent, silence and the domain-restricted fix. The versions and multiplier results reuse the same pattern. Everything here is a synthetic fixture; the project formalizes no real interface.
sizeNote: About 1,300 lines of Lean in 18 files (about 800 of them in the proof core this site covers), plus four cached LRAT certificates.
agentCtx: etc-fp-bitexact (Evolving Technologies Corporation): a Mathlib-free Lean 4 demo that models binary16 bit patterns as BitVec 16, builds interface-compatibility propositions from mock ICD fixtures, and discharges them with bv_decide/bv_check against cached LRAT certificates.

gloss.BitVec: BitVec n (Lean core): a fixed-width word of n bits. Arithmetic wraps around modulo 2n, and &&&, |||, ^^^, <<< are bitwise AND, OR, XOR and shift-left.
gloss.Bool: Bool: the two values true/false. Here it doubles as the flush-to-zero flag.
gloss.Not: ¬ P: P is false (formally, P implies False).
gloss.Ne: a ≠ b: a and b are different values.
gloss.Exists: ∃ x, P x: some x satisfies P. The proof here names it explicitly.
gloss.True: True: the trivially true proposition, proved by True.intro.
